title: Waacking
subtitle: Arms first, then the turns, then the attitude that holds it together.
description: Waacking came out of the 1970s Los Angeles disco clubs: whipping arm rotations, sharp poses and musicality that plays the record rather than the count. The arms carry the style, but they only read if the stance underneath them is quiet — so the path builds the frame before it builds the speed. Work it slowly. Every whip here is a shape you can hold at quarter tempo before it is a whip.

stages.title: What the style is
stages.description: Watch before drilling. Waacking has a vocabulary and a history, and the moves make more sense once you know which part of the dance they belong to.

steps.title: Waacking, end to end
steps.description: A full beginner tutorial in one sitting — rotations, poses and the disco they belong to. Come back to this whenever a later step stops making sense on its own.

steps.title: Whack, punk and pose
steps.description: The three things the style is made of: the whip of the arm, the character you play, and the shape you land on. Almost everything below is one of these three.

steps.title: Root the stance
steps.description: Weight slightly forward, knees soft, shoulders down and still. Every whip you throw is only as sharp as the body that stays put behind it. Drill it in a mirror with the arms hanging dead.

stages.title: The arm
stages.description: The signature of the style, learned slowly. Speed comes from the path being clean, not from throwing harder.

steps.title: The waack
steps.description: A wide circular arm throw from the shoulder, not the elbow. Trace the circle at quarter speed until the path is identical every time.

steps.title: The arm roll
steps.description: A continuous rotation that never stops at the top. This is the connective tissue — without it the dance is a series of unrelated shapes.

steps.title: Single arm roll, right
steps.description: The roll isolated on one side, broken all the way down. Four minutes on one arm; it is worth every second.

steps.title: Single arm roll, left
steps.description: The same on your weaker side. Do not skip it — waacking reads as lopsided the moment one arm is behind the other.

stages.title: Speed
stages.description: Same paths, more of them per bar. Add tempo only once the shape survives it.

steps.title: Quick arms
steps.description: The roll tightened until it snaps. The circle gets smaller, not sloppier.

steps.title: Medium tempo
steps.description: First pass at speed. If the elbow starts leading, drop back to the single-arm breakdown.

steps.title: Fast tempo
steps.description: Disco tempo. At this point the arm should be running on shape memory, leaving your attention free for the record.

steps.title: Doubles and triples
steps.description: Two and three whips inside one beat. Practise against a metronome before a track — the temptation is always to rush the second one.

stages.title: Rotation
stages.description: Where the arms and the floor start negotiating. The body turns; the arm keeps its path.

steps.title: Flicks with rotation
steps.description: Whip the arm and let the body pivot a quarter turn with it. The first place the two halves have to cooperate.

steps.title: Whip out of a turn
steps.description: Land the rotation and throw on the exit, not during. Turning and whipping at once reads as a stumble; turning then whipping reads as a hit.

stages.title: Footwork underneath
stages.description: Waacking is not danced standing still. These keep the lower half alive while the arms do the talking.

steps.title: Footwork and arm placement
steps.description: How the feet and the arms agree with each other. The section to rewatch when your arms look right but the dance looks static.

steps.title: The heel-toe
steps.description: Rocking between heel and ball of the foot. Small, quiet, and it gives the arms something to travel over.

steps.title: Sous-sous
steps.description: A tight rise onto both balls of the feet, borrowed straight from ballet. Waacking leans on ballet vocabulary more than any other club style.

steps.title: Walks and struts
steps.description: Crossing the floor in character. The runway walk is half the performance in a battle and it is almost never drilled.

stages.title: Turns
stages.description: Rotation on a fixed axis, so the arms can hold their shape all the way through.

steps.title: En dehors
steps.description: The outward turn. Spot it properly before adding any arm — a whip out of a wobbly turn reads as an accident.

steps.title: The inverted turn
steps.description: A turn on the ball of one foot with the other leg extended. Combines the footwork above with the arm path from stage two.

stages.title: Pose and perform
stages.description: The part that cannot be drilled — it is decided by the record.

steps.title: Posing
steps.description: Every phrase of whips ends on a held shape. Poses are what the audience actually remembers, and they are the cheapest thing on this path to get good at.

steps.title: Put it all together
steps.description: Rolls, quick arms and a pose strung into one phrase. The first thing on this path that looks like dancing rather than drilling.

steps.title: Practice with music
steps.description: The same material over a real track. Notice how much of your timing was coming from the count rather than the song.

steps.title: Freestyle rounds
steps.description: Ninety seconds of disco, no plan. Waacking is a battle style — the goal is reacting to the record in real time, not recalling a combo.
